opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that a direct comparison in raw numbers is a little misleading, because the two kinds of data are doing very different jobs. If you just count tokens or hours, robotic data looks tiny next to the internet. Even the largest robot datasets people have put together are orders of magnitude smaller than what goes into pretraining a frontier language model. So if the question is "are we going to catch up to internet scale by brute force teleoperation," probably not anytime soon, and I don't think that's the right goal.

The way I think about it is that internet data gives you a kind of prior: knowledge about the world, about objects, about what people mean when they say "put the dishes away," some sense of physics and common sense. What it doesn't give you is the embodied part, the closed-loop experience of actually acting, seeing the consequences, and correcting. That's the thing that robot data uniquely supplies. And it turns out you need a lot less of it than you'd think, if you're building on top of a strong pretrained model, because you're not learning everything from scratch. You're learning how to ground knowledge the model already has into physical behavior.

The other piece is that robot data has a property internet data mostly doesn't: once robots are deployed and doing useful work, they generate their own experience. That's where I think the real scaling story is. It's not about humans laboriously collecting demonstrations forever; it's about getting to the point where the system is good enough to be useful, so it gets deployed, and then the deployment itself produces data, including the mistakes and recoveries, which are actually the most valuable part. That's a flywheel that language models don't quite have in the same way.

So I'd say the gap in volume is real, but the more important question is whether you can get to that flywheel. If you can, the amount of embodied experience can grow very quickly, and the comparison to internet data starts to look a lot less lopsided.

r001.rationale: It says raw counts are misleading because the data do different jobs, but does not identify correlation between robotic time steps as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It says less robot data may be needed with a strong pretrained model, but does not claim robotic data has lower information density per byte.

r003.rationale: It contrasts robot data with internet data generally and does not propose multimodal datasets as the better comparison.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a really interesting question, and I think the honest answer is that it's kind of apples and oranges in a way that's actually pretty important to understand.

So if you just count bytes, or count hours, the comparison looks terrible for robotics. Internet-scale text is on the order of trillions of tokens. The video that these vision-language models are trained on is, you know, essentially a big chunk of YouTube. And the robot datasets that we have, even the biggest ones, the ones that we've put together at Physical Intelligence, or Open X-Embodiment before that, are something like thousands or tens of thousands of hours. So if you're measuring by raw quantity, we're many orders of magnitude behind, and that's not going to close any time soon by just collecting more robot data.

But I think that framing is a little misleading, for a couple of reasons.

The first is that the relevant question isn't really "how much data do you have," it's "how much data do you have per unit of what you need to learn." And a lot of what a robot needs to know, it doesn't actually have to learn from robot data. It needs to know what objects are, how they roughly behave, what a kitchen looks like, what the word "put the dishes away" means, what the plausible sequence of steps is. All of that is in the internet data, and it gets inherited when you build the robot policy on top of a vision-language model. So the robot data is not carrying the whole load. It's carrying the part that's actually specific to embodiment: how the physics of contact works, what it feels like to grasp something, how to translate an intention into joint commands at fifty hertz. That part is a much narrower thing than "all of intelligence," and so it's reasonable that it would need a much smaller dataset.

The second thing is that the robot data is much denser in the signal we care about. If you think about a random hour of YouTube, the fraction of it that's about manipulation, about physical interaction in a way that's useful to a robot, is tiny. Whereas every second of robot data is directly about the thing. So the effective data, the amount of information about the task distribution, is a lot closer than the raw numbers suggest.

And then the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is that the quality of the comparison depends on what you're trying to do. If what you want is a model that can reason about the world in language, then yeah, the internet is the right benchmark and robots will never catch up. But what we want is a model that can act, and for that there's no substitute. There's no internet of actions. Nobody uploaded their motor commands to YouTube. So in some sense the question isn't "how do we match the internet," it's "what's the minimum amount of embodied experience we need, given that everything else comes from elsewhere." And my sense is that the answer is a lot smaller than people assume.

Now, the place where I think the analogy does hold up, and where we should be a little humble, is the scaling story. In language, the thing that worked was that the data was already there, and you just needed the compute and the architecture to absorb it. In robotics, we're in this weird situation where we have to create the data at the same time that we're figuring out how to learn from it. And those two things feed back into each other, because a better model lets you collect data more efficiently, and more data lets you build a better model. So I actually think the right mental model isn't "robotics is where language was in 2015 with less data," it's more like we're running the data flywheel and the model flywheel at the same time, and the interesting question is how fast that loop spins.

r001.rationale: The response discusses raw data volume and task relevance but does not identify correlation between robotic time steps as an obstacle to comparison.

r002.rationale: It says robot data is denser in useful signal than internet video, the opposite of comparatively low information density per byte.

r003.rationale: It mentions video and vision-language models but does not propose multimodal training datasets as a better comparison for robotic experience data.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to be careful about is what unit you’re using to compare them. You could take a robot’s video stream, count up all the pixels, and end up with a very large number of bytes. But consecutive frames are highly correlated. That doesn’t mean you have the equivalent of that many bytes of text from the internet.

The more meaningful question is how much diversity of experience you have. How many different situations has the robot encountered? How many different things has it tried? By that measure, the amount of robotic data we have is still very small compared to internet data. A robot can spend a whole day collecting experience in one room, manipulating a handful of objects. There’s a lot of data there, but it covers a very narrow slice of the world.

On the other hand, robotic experience gives you something that internet data generally doesn’t: you take an action and observe what happens. That’s particularly valuable if what you’re trying to learn is how to act. So I don’t think there’s a clean conversion factor between the two.

The opportunity is to combine them. We’d like the robot to inherit as much as possible from models trained on internet data—knowledge about objects, language, and some aspects of the physical world—and use robotic experience to learn how to turn that knowledge into behavior. Then the question becomes how much additional interaction you need to bridge that gap, rather than whether we can reproduce the entire scale of internet pretraining with robots.

r001.rationale: It says consecutive video frames are highly correlated, so counting them as independent data overstates the comparison.

r002.rationale: It explains that a large byte count of robot video does not equal the same amount of internet text, indicating lower information density per byte.

r003.rationale: It proposes combining internet-trained models with robotic experience, but does not suggest multimodal training datasets as the better comparison.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be a little careful about what you're counting. A robot might collect observations at thirty frames a second, but those aren't thirty independent examples. And an hour of a robot repeatedly doing the same thing is very different from an hour of video that contains lots of different objects, environments, and behaviors. So the number of frames or the number of bytes is probably not the most useful comparison. The diversity of the experience matters enormously.

The other distinction is what that data can teach you. Internet data can tell you a tremendous amount about what the world looks like and what people do in it. But a robot also needs to understand how its own actions affect the world. If I apply this force, does the object move, does it slip, do I lose my grasp? Observing somebody else doing something doesn't necessarily resolve those questions.

So I wouldn't frame the goal as collecting enough robot data to match the internet. I would frame it as using internet-scale pretraining to acquire as much general knowledge as possible, and then using robotic experience to learn the parts that aren't adequately specified by that knowledge. The big question is how much interaction you need to make that connection, and how well that interaction generalizes across tasks and environments.

r001.rationale: It says robot frames are not independent examples and contrasts repetitive robot activity with more varied video, identifying dependence as a problem when comparing data volume.

r002.rationale: It says bytes are not a useful comparison and emphasizes diversity, but does not clearly claim robotic experience has lower information density per byte.

r003.rationale: It discusses internet data and robot interaction, but does not propose multimodal training datasets as a better comparison.
